1.pericope_label: And Jacob lifted up his eyes, and looked, and, behold, Esau came, and with him four hundred men. And he divided the children unto Leah, and unto Rachel, and unto the two handmaids. And he put the handmaids and their children foremost, and Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph hindermost. And he passed over before them, and bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.

schools.summary: Keep Jacob's fear reasonable rather than faithless: his brother had still the same cause of hatred as before, and it was not probable that after leaving his father's house and living as he pleased he had grown milder, so that terror at Esau's approach was not merely renewed but increased. Read the ordering of the family as prudence under danger, the wives and children placed so that if anything hostile were attempted the whole seed should not perish but part have time for flight; but refuse to defend the placing of Rachel and Joseph last, since the substance of the benediction lay in Judah — excusing the man only because that oracle had not yet been revealed, and saying plainly that he was excessively indulgent to Rachel. Then take the sevenfold bowing as worship offered to God rather than honour paid to a man, on the ground that it was completed before Esau came near, while noting the objection that everything before and after indicates civil reverence, which took nothing from the prerogative of the covenant.

Attack the assumption that Esau came with hostile intent: there is no kind of evidence for it, no proof that the four hundred men were armed at all, and every proof that he behaved with openness and candour and with a forgetfulness of past injuries of which only a great mind is capable — so ask why this man's character should be perpetually vilified, and answer that it serves a system in which he must be a reprobate and therefore everything bad. On the arrangement of the family, offer two motives without choosing between them: either apprehension, setting foremost those least esteemed so that if the front met with evil the rest might escape on swift beasts, or calculation, keeping the choicest treasure to the last so that Rachel and Joseph should make the deeper impression. Record simply that he feared Esau as an enemy and did obeisance to him as an elder brother.

Read the going first as courage rather than calculation: while providing some small chance of escape for wives and children arranged according to their rank, Jacob manfully went before them and placed himself entirely in Esau's power. Explain why the obeisance was needed at all, since the cause of the quarrel had been his usurpation of the right of precedence belonging to the firstborn, so that the sevenfold bowing was an acknowledgment of Esau's superiority offered to propitiate him; and describe the gesture as it is made in the East, by bending the body forward with the arms crossed and the right hand held over the heart.

Take the lifting of the eyes for cheerfulness and confidence rather than a dejected countenance, since a man who has committed his case to God by prayer goes on his way with his countenance no more sad, and those who have cast their care upon him may look before them with composure, cheerfully expecting the issue whatever it prove. Then contrast the two brothers as they appear: Esau attended with a guard of four hundred men and looking big, Jacob followed by a cumbersome train of women and children who are his care and looking tender and solicitous for their safety — and yet Jacob had the birthright and was every way the better man. Note that it is no disparagement to great and good men to attend personally to their families, and that Jacob at the head of his household set a better example than Esau at the head of his regiment.

debates.question: Did Esau come with hostile intent?

sides.position: No: there is no evidence of hostility, no proof the four hundred were armed, and every proof of openness and candour — the vilifying of his character serves a system
Yes, so far as Jacob could judge: his brother had the same cause of hatred as before, and it was not probable that living as he pleased had made him milder
The question is left open; what the lifting of the eyes shows is cheerfulness in a man who had committed his case to God

debates.question: Why were the wives and children ordered so?

sides.position: For safety, so that if anything hostile were attempted the whole seed should not perish but part have time for flight — though the placing of Rachel last was excessive indulgence
Either apprehension, setting foremost those least esteemed, or calculation, keeping the choicest treasure to be seen last
As a matter of rank, while Jacob himself went first and placed himself entirely in Esau's power
Because the handmaids were less honourable and less beloved
God, in thanks and in supplication, since the bowing was finished before Esau came near
Esau, as civil reverence acknowledging his superiority in the matter of precedence that had caused the quarrel
Esau, as an elder brother, though feared as an enemy

outliers.note: Alone mounts a defence of Esau’s character, arguing that the assumption of hostile intent has no evidence behind it and survives because it serves a system in which Esau must be a reprobate.
Alone faults Jacob for the order of the march, holding that the placing of Rachel and Joseph last was excessive indulgence, since the substance of the benediction lay in Judah.

themes: Esau came, and with him four hundred men

4.pericope_label: And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept. And he lifted up his eyes, and saw the women and the children; and said, Who are those with thee? And he said, The children which God hath graciously given thy servant. Then the handmaidens came near, they and their children, and they bowed themselves. And Leah also with her children came near, and bowed themselves: and after came Joseph near and Rachel, and they bowed themselves.

schools.summary: Make the unexpected benevolence the effect of special favour, God proving by this method that he has the hearts of men in his hand, to soften their hardness and mitigate their cruelty when he pleases, taming them as wild beasts are tamed, and hearkening to the prayers of his servant — so that when the threats of enemies alarm us we should resort to this sacred anchor. Distinguish two ways the thing may work, since God does not always incline cruel minds to humanity but sometimes merely restrains them from harm while they rage; and allow that Esau's malice may have been under constraint with humanity gaining a temporary ascendancy, as the Egyptians were driven to a moment's humanity while being nothing better than before. Then draw the confession out of the answer about the children, that they are not so produced by nature as to overturn the declaration that the fruit of the womb is a reward, since if the fecundity of brute animals is God's gift much more is that of men made in his image.

Call the conduct sincere, genuine and magnanimous, since Esau had buried all his resentment and forgotten his injuries and received his brother with the strongest demonstrations not only of forgiveness but of fraternal affection. Report that in the Masoretic Bibles each letter of the word for kissing is dotted to make it emphatic, and take the rabbis to have meant by that notation to draw attention to the change in Esau and the sincerity of his welcome. On the softening itself, say that God can of a sudden convert enemies into friends, instancing two men of the same name changed the one by restraining and the other by renewing grace; and divide the causes of the weeping, Jacob's tears being for joy at the reception and Esau's perhaps for grief and shame at the design he had once conceived.

Hold that whatever Esau's intention when he set out, the sight of his brother brought back the old times of their childhood and overcame him with love, and that he never afterwards seems to have wavered in fraternal affection, being a man of warm feelings as an earlier scene had already shown. Report the extraordinary vowels attached to the word for kissing and the supposition built on them, that the Masorites meant to signify the kiss was not a sign of genuine love — and say roundly that for such an ill-natured supposition there is no warrant whatsoever. Render the question about the women and children literally as who are these belonging to thee, an enquiry for fuller information about a family plainly Jacob's.

Notice that the account Jacob had sent ahead of the increase of his estate said nothing of children, perhaps so as not to expose them to his brother's rage if he came as an enemy, or to please him with the unexpected sight if he came as a friend, so that the question was a natural one. Then weigh the answer given: it would have been enough to say they were his children, and fit enough for a profane hearer, but then he would not have spoken like a man whose eyes were ever toward the Lord. Take the reply as making two claims at once, that the children are God's gifts and that they are choice gifts, accounted great blessings though many, much his care, and as yet but slenderly provided for; and observe that it becomes us not only to do common actions but to speak of them after a godly sort.

debates.question: What do the scribal points over the word for kissing mean?

sides.position: That the word is emphatic, the rabbis drawing attention to the change in Esau and the sincerity of his welcome
The Masorites are supposed to signify that the kiss was not genuine — an ill-natured supposition for which there is no warrant whatsoever
By special favour: God has the hearts of men in his hand and tames them as wild beasts are tamed, though he may only restrain a cruelty still pent up, as with the Egyptians
Because God can of a sudden convert enemies into friends, whether by restraining or by renewing grace
Because the sight of his brother brought back the old times of their childhood in a man of warm feelings

outliers.note: Alone contradicts the received account of the scribal points over the word for kissing, denying that they were meant to impugn the kiss and calling the supposition ill-natured and unwarranted.

Alone allows that Esau’s cruelty may merely have been under restraint with humanity gaining a temporary ascendancy, comparing the Egyptians who were driven to a moment’s humanity while being nothing better than before.

themes: the children which God hath graciously given

8.pericope_label: And he said, What meanest thou by all this drove which I met? And he said, These are to find grace in the sight of my lord. And Esau said, I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself. And Jacob said, Nay, I pray thee, if now I have found grace in thy sight, then receive my present at my hand: for therefore I have seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God, and thou wast pleased with me. Take, I pray thee, my blessing that is brought to thee; because God hath dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough. And he urged him, and he took it.

schools.summary: Observe that the word Esau uses is the proper term for an encampment of pastoral people with their flocks, the same rendered bands and company earlier and current in the narrative ever since Mahanaim, so that the five droves might naturally remind him of cattle driven in at evening. Read his refusal as generosity rather than coldness, since he wished to spare his brother so large a present and was himself rich, while noting that to refuse outright would have been a mark of hostility. Explain the comparison to the face of God as containing much oriental hyperbole and yet no irreverence, since to the Hebrew the thought of God was not terrifying and the sight of his face was the sight of something good; what the phrase conveys is that Esau used his power as generously as God is wont to use his, and Jacob might say it without cringing because he discerned God's work in the change. Keep the word blessing narrow, as the present expressive of a desire to bless, and note the claim to have all rather than merely much, made as heir of the divine promise.

Explain the question as a way of declining rather than a request for information, since when a thing does not please us we are apt to ask about it as though it were unknown; and note that Jacob is urgent and does not cease asking until his brother receives the gift, because the acceptance was to be a pledge of reconciliation. Meet the difficulty in the comparison of Esau's face to God's, raising the objection oneself — that it seems to wrong God by likening him to a reprobate, and to be false besides, since given the choice Jacob would have avoided the meeting — and untie both knots by the Hebrew habit of calling whatever is excellent divine, and by observing that Esau thus changed was no obscure figure of God's favour. On the word blessing, allow it actively of the goodwill testified or passively of what God has bestowed and is now imparted, then turn the verse on the reader: nearly the same words are on all tongues while few truly ascribe to God what they possess, the greater part sacrificing to their own industry.

Supply the custom that makes the exchange intelligible: in eastern countries a present received by a superior is a pledge of friendship while a present refused leaves everything to be feared, so that Jacob was urgent precisely because acceptance would oblige his brother to treat him as a friend thereafter. Note that he could not be certain of having found favour until the gift was taken. Reduce the comparison with the face of God to its plain sense, that he had seen his brother reconciled to him and at peace with him as he desired to see God reconciled; and observe that a gift was reckoned lucky and God the giver of all good luck, which is why it is called a blessing.

debates.question: Why did Esau ask what the drove meant?

sides.position: Not from ignorance but to refuse the gift, since we ask about what does not please us as though it were unknown
From generosity, wishing to spare his brother so large a present, knowing well what the five herds were

debates.question: How can Esau's face be compared to the face of God?

sides.position: By the Hebrew habit of calling whatever is excellent divine, and because Esau thus changed was no obscure figure of God's favour
Because Jacob discerned God's work in the change and saw in his brother's friendliness a reflection of the divine, so he might say it without cringing
It is oriental hyperbole but not irreverence, since to the Hebrew the face of God was the sight of something good
It means only that he saw his brother reconciled to him as he desired to see God reconciled

outliers.note: Alone supplies the eastern custom that makes the exchange intelligible, that a present received by a superior is a pledge of friendship while one refused leaves everything to be feared.

Alone defends the comparison with the face of God as historically natural, observing that God was nearer to men in those simple days than now that science has revealed the immensity of his attributes.

themes: what meanest thou by all this drove
as though I had seen the face of God

12.pericope_label: And he said, Let us take our journey, and let us go, and I will go before thee. And he said unto him, My lord knoweth that the children are tender, and the flocks and herds with young are with me: and if men should overdrive them one day, all the flock will die. Let my lord, I pray thee, pass over before his servant: and I will lead on softly, according as the cattle that goeth before me and the children be able to endure, until I come unto my lord unto Seir. And Esau said, Let me now leave with thee some of the folk that are with me. And he said, What needeth it? let me find grace in the sight of my lord.

schools.summary: Explain the difficulty exactly: the flocks and herds in question are those giving milk, which is why they are an object of especial anxiety, and a caravan with delicate children and cattle needing care could not keep pace with a company of horsemen without taking harm, so that overdriving them a single day would kill the sheep. Deny that the refusal sprang from distrust and that the ground assigned was a pretext, since a military guard was unnecessary to a man who knew himself defended by the hosts of God. Correct the rendering of the clause about pace, which is literally the foot of the cattle and of the children, and note the ages — Joseph only six or seven, Leah's younger sons too tender for much fatigue. Report the inference that the season was winter, drawn from the phrase about flocks that give suck and thought to be confirmed by the folds at Succoth, while calling the conclusion uncertain and suggesting the halt was rather because of the lameness.

Grant that Jacob feared no perfidy hidden under the garb of friendship but was cautiously avoiding fresh occasions of offence, since a proud and ferocious man may be exasperated again by light causes; and yet do not deny that his anxiety was excessive, asking whence such an incredible change of mind in Esau could have come unless he had been divinely transformed from a wolf into a lamb, and drawing the lesson that we should restrain our anxieties rather than tremble over an affair God has already provided for. Then charge the promise about Seir: the reasons alleged are true but introduced under false pretexts, since he afterwards turned his journey in another direction and so promised what he was not intending to do — and press the principle that truth is so precious to God that he will not allow us to lie or deceive even when no injury follows. Note also that the eldest child was about thirteen and the youngest about six, and that Esau could see by their stature they were not able to bear fast travelling.

Read the offer of company as a token of sincere reconciliation and marvel at it, since the brothers were never so loving as now and God made Esau not merely not an enemy but a friend, so that we should never despair of any nor distrust the God in whose hand all hearts are. Then defend Jacob's sincerity about Seir: he was very likely perfectly sincere in the expressed purpose, and circumstances afterwards made the visit improper or impracticable, or else it was made once his concerns elsewhere were settled though it is not recorded; and note that Esau later removed to Canaan, where the brothers dwelt together for years. On the escort declined, hold that those are sufficiently guarded who have God for their guard and are under convoy of his hosts, and read the closing words as meaning that with his brother's favour Jacob had all he desired from him.

debates.question: Was Jacob sincere in promising to follow to Seir?

sides.position: No: the reasons alleged were true but urged under false pretexts, since he turned his journey elsewhere; truth is so precious to God that he forbids deceit even where no injury follows
Yes: he was very likely perfectly sincere, and circumstances afterwards made the visit improper or impracticable
Yes, and we may presume the visit was made once his concerns were settled, though it is not recorded
Yes in purpose, but not carried out, probably because Esau had not yet settled there
Not from distrust, and the ground given was no pretext: a military guard was unnecessary to a man defended by the hosts of God
To avoid fresh occasions of offence, though the anxiety was excessive in a man for whom God had already provided
Because those are sufficiently guarded who have God for their guard
The men were offered to show the way, guard the road, and make Jacob appear more honourable entering Seir

outliers.note: Alone charges Jacob with deceit over the promise to follow to Seir, and presses the principle that truth is so precious to God that he forbids deception even where no injury follows — a charge his own editor prints a rebuttal to.
Alone reports the inference that the season was winter, drawn from the phrase about flocks giving suck and the making of folds at Succoth, while judging the conclusion uncertain.

themes: until I come unto my lord unto Seir

16.pericope_label: So Esau returned that day on his way unto Seir. And Jacob journeyed to Succoth, and built him an house, and made booths for his cattle: therefore the name of the place is called Succoth.

schools.summary: Fix the site by argument rather than tradition: since Jacob crossed a ford of the Jordan after leaving Succoth, the place cannot have belonged to Canaan and must lie east of the river. Weigh the two claimants, one in the tribe of Gad in the corner formed by the Jordan and the Jabbok, the other still called Sakut on the western bank, and reject the second because it lies ten miles north of the junction and Jacob would hardly go so far out of his way. Then make an argument from the building itself, since cattle in that country remain in the open air the whole year round, so that making folds for them is quite unusual and the fact that the spot kept the name of the booths shows the thing was noticed at the time — a strong though undesigned testimony to the truth of the narrative. Reconstruct the reason for the halt from the preceding weeks: pursued by Laban, worn by anxiety and a hurried removal, facing a greater danger in front, wrestling all night instead of resting, moving forward at sunrise with a sprained hip, enduring the interview agitated by fear and hope and joy, and then, the danger over, breaking down.

Note that the name is used here by anticipation, no city yet standing on the spot, and place it in a valley within the territory of Sihon king of Heshbon, afterwards allotted to Gad and mentioned in company with Penuel, reported only two miles away though that distance seems too short. Then explain why the memorial was fixed here and nowhere else: Jacob had found no quiet resting-place until he came thither, and though he had pitched tents in many places along the way, on this one alone he set the record of divine grace, because here at length it was granted him to remain in some abode, not having dared before to plant his foot firmly anywhere. Add that Esau took his leave the same day he met his brother and set out for Seir, though whether he arrived within the day is uncertain.

Turn the name forward into the nation's memory: the place afterwards became a city beyond Jordan in the tribe of Gad, and since its name means booths, when his posterity came to dwell in houses of stone they might remember that a Syrian ready to perish was their father, a man glad of booths, that being the rock from which they were hewn. Note also that having parted from his brother in a friendly manner he came at last, after a perilous journey full of difficulties, safely into Canaan — and that diseases and dangers should teach us to value health and safety and enlarge our hearts in thankfulness when our going out and coming in have been signally preserved.

Derive the name from the booths erected there for the resting and convenience of the family, and suppose the stay a long one, the household in all probability continuing there for a considerable time.

sides.position: East of the Jordan, since Jacob crossed a ford after leaving it, so it did not belong to Canaan
In the corner formed by the Jordan and the Jabbok, not the western Sakut, which lies ten miles out of the way
In a valley in the territory of Sihon, afterwards allotted to Gad and named with Penuel

debates.question: Why did Jacob stop and build there?

sides.position: Because he had found no quiet resting-place till then, and fixed the memorial of grace where he might at last remain
Because he had broken down after weeks of terror, a wrestling night and a sprained hip, once the danger was past
For the resting and convenience of the family, who probably continued there a considerable time

outliers.note: Alone builds an argument for the narrative’s truthfulness out of the folds, since cattle in that country stay in the open air all year, so that making shelters was unusual enough to be remembered in the name; and alone reconstructs the halt as a physical breakdown after weeks of strain.
Alone turns the name forward into the nation’s memory, that when the posterity dwelt in houses of stone they might remember a father glad of booths.

themes: Esau returned that day unto Seir

18.pericope_label: And Jacob came to Shalem, a city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Padan–aram; and pitched his tent before the city. And he bought a parcel of a field, where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for an hundred pieces of money. And he erected there an altar, and called it El–elohe–Israel.

schools.summary: Take Shalem as an adjective and not a place, meaning whole or sound, and refine the common rendering, since in peace would not mean peaceably but that his troubles were at an end and his lameness cured — a sense in which Rashi also saw an allusion to the healing of the limp. Draw the conclusion that gives the verse its weight, that the word answers the vow made at Bethel before he left Canaan, so that what Jacob had asked for was now fulfilled and he had returned in safety to the land. Set the purchase in a series, since Abraham a century earlier had to buy a burial place from an owner who could give him title, and Jacob must now buy even the ground to pitch his tent, which would be required only near a town; note that this first parcel is where Joseph's embalmed body was afterwards buried and that possession of it stayed secure while the owners were in Egypt. Hold that the unit of price was plainly an ingot of some value, on the evidence of the Book of Job, and that for the rendering lambs there is no support. Read the altar as thankoffering, as taking possession, and chiefly as a profession of faith, which is why the name given it acknowledges the new name its builder had just received.

Canvass the candidate towns and reject both Jerusalem, as forty miles off, and the Salem of Melchizedek, while reporting that the Jewish writers generally take the word of his coming in peace and health. Note that he bought a part of a field and not the whole, and that though heir of the country he bought at all because the time for possession was not yet come. Then explain what an altar was for, lest anyone think the patriarchs trifled with worship: under the word understand the external testimony of piety, the offering of victims and invoking of the name by a pure rite handed down from Noah and Shem. Find in it a measure of the man, that though broken down by various troubles he was not forgetful of the altar, and did not content himself with worshipping privately in the secret feeling of his mind, since men want helps while they are in the flesh; and add the domestic motive, that a pious father must take care his house is not profane but that God reigns in it as in a sanctuary.

Render the disputed word in peace or in safety and deny it is a city name, being found nowhere else, citing the older English translators with the Chaldee and the Arabic in agreement; and observe that after resting at Succoth he reached a city of Shechem in health of body, without loss of cattle or servants, his wives and children also safe. On the price, report the long and learned discussion, that the word signifies a lamb so that a hundred lambs may be meant, and canvass the conjecture that the coin bore a lamb's figure and took its name from the stamp, illustrating from coins named for their images and from the Athenian piece stamped with an ox. Suggest rendering the altar's name as the strong God is the God of Israel, referring to the change of the builder's own name; and draw the reflections that when a man's ways please God he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him, and that the first thing pious men do is to provide for the honour and worship of God.

debates.question: Is Shalem a place or a description?

sides.position: A description: in peace or in safety, and not likely a city name, being found nowhere else
An adjective answering the vow at Bethel, so that what Jacob asked before leaving Canaan was now fulfilled
An adjective meaning whole or sound, better rendered in good condition, with an allusion to the cure of his lameness
Possibly a place, though the Jewish writers generally take it of his coming in peace and health
Possibly a hundred lambs, or coins stamped with a lamb and named from the image, as other coins are named for theirs
An ingot of metal of considerable value, on the evidence of Job; for the rendering lambs there is no support

outliers.note: Alone ties the word to the vow made at Bethel before the departure from Canaan, so that the verse records the fulfilment of what Jacob had asked.
Alone pursues the name of the coin through comparative numismatics, from the Athenian piece stamped with an ox to the English angel and the Portuguese joe, all named for the images they bore.

themes: Jacob came to Shalem, a city of Shechem
